How many deals does the bot need to imagine?

Tricks 2, 3, 4 · M3 early-trick yardstick (M3-SPEC §13.1 item 10) · made by search curves and python/tools/ncurves_report.py

The question. When the bot chooses a card it imagines N possible deals [complete guesses of where the hidden cards are], solves each one exactly, and plays the card that does best on average. More deals means a better choice but more time. How much money chance does a bot with N deals give away, per decision, compared with a bot that could imagine every possible deal? And how many deals are needed to keep that loss below 0.01%, 0.005% or 0.002% money chance?

(For scale: 0.01% money chance is a 1-in-10,000 chance of the match, about 0.0008 stakes per team per decision, 0.0004 per player, since a match swings 8 stakes for a team: each player wins 3 or loses 1.)

The short answer

  • Hand features (details): the clear differences in deals needed: two or more voids rather than one at trick 3 (3.1×, range 1.6–6.6×); being the robber at trick 4 (2.6×, range 1.1–5.8×). The other comparisons have ranges on both sides of 1, so these samples cannot call them yet.
  • The loss shrinks like a power of N: loss = a × N−b. Each scenario has its own size a; one exponent b is shared by all scenarios of a trick, as asked. With b around 0.7–0.8, doubling the deals cuts the loss by roughly 40–45%. (If b were 1, doubling would halve it.)
  • Trick 2: a 10-deal choice differs from the 320-deal choice in 34% of decisions, yet costs only 0.106% money chance on average; even 160 deals still differ in 12%. Changed choices are nearly always near-ties. The 320-deal yardstick itself is predicted to lose about 0.0082% per decision (range 0.0040%–0.0142%).
  • Trick 3: a 10-deal choice differs from the 320-deal choice in 30% of decisions, yet costs only 0.081% money chance on average; even 160 deals still differ in 11%. Changed choices are nearly always near-ties. The 320-deal yardstick itself is predicted to lose about 0.0067% per decision (range 0.0030%–0.0123%).
  • Trick 4: a 10-deal choice differs from the 320-deal choice in 17% of decisions, yet costs only 0.041% money chance on average; even 160 deals still differ in 4%. Changed choices are nearly always near-ties. The 320-deal yardstick itself is predicted to lose about 0.0026% per decision (range 0.0010%–0.0059%).
  • This is why the agreement report's plateau rule (fewer than 1% of choices change when the deals are doubled) is never met on these grids: choices keep flipping between near-equal cards long after the money at stake is negligible. The money-loss threshold is the useful yardstick.
  • Predictions for the stricter thresholds lie beyond the 320 deals actually measured, so their ranges are wide. The extension tool (search worlds --ids … --from-world 320) can measure chosen scenarios at 640 or more deals to check them.

How the measurement works

Re-using the saved deals. Every decision was solved exactly in 320 deals. To see what a bot with N deals would have done, we pick N of the 320 at random, let the bot choose with those, and repeat this 400 times. No new solving is needed, so any N up to 320 can be checked.

A fair referee. To score a choice we need to know which card is truly best, and we only have 320 deals to judge with. If the same deals are used both to choose and to judge, the judge flatters the choice: near 320 the "loss" drops to zero simply because the player and the judge saw the same deals (the grey crosses in the charts show this). So each repetition splits the 320 deals in two halves. The bot's N-deal choice and a careful 160-deal choice are both made from the first half, and both are scored on the second half, which neither has seen. On average this measures exactly how much worse the N-deal choice is than the 160-deal choice, with no flattering. The fitted curve then adds back what the 160-deal choice itself still loses, which gives the total loss against a perfect bot.

How sure we are. The ranges come from re-drawing the set of decisions 1,000 times (keeping the same mix of positions and match situations) and redoing every step. They cover both which decisions happened to be picked and which deals happened to be drawn.

Checks. (1) Held out: the curve is fitted only on N up to 80, and must predict N from 90 to 150. (2) Extrapolation: the whole recipe is rerun using only the first 160 deals of each decision (so its own measurements stop at 80), and it must predict what the full 320 deals show, up to N = 150 — this is the honest test of predicting beyond the measured range.

Each group's own exponent is uncertain because each group has only about 50–100 decisions. Most groups' own ranges include the shared value; the exceptions: trick 2 pos3 (own b 1.24, range 0.75–1.90): its loss falls faster than the shared curve says, so its predicted N errs on the safe (high) side; trick 3 pos6 (own b 1.05, range 0.74–1.39): its loss falls faster than the shared curve says, so its predicted N errs on the safe (high) side; trick 4 pos6 (own b 1.76, range 0.95–2.75): its loss falls faster than the shared curve says, so its predicted N errs on the safe (high) side.

The 5 of trumps, robbing and voids

Three more facts about the deciding player's hand, each something the player can see for themselves (owner, 2026-10-14): whether they hold the 5 of trumps (the bonus card), whether they are the robber (they took a turned card this hand: robbed it with the ace of trumps, or, as dealer, robbed a turned ace or took a turned Joker), and how many plain suits they are void in [hold no card of]. Partners always sit across, so there is no feature for that. These were worked out again from the saved decisions (each one replayed from its deal and the cards played), so nothing was solved again.

Groups with fewer than 25 decisions are left out of the chart (the no-void group at tricks 3 and 4). Deals needed for an expected loss of 0.01% per decision, with the 95% range in brackets:

The holders of the 5 and the robbers are only 38–52 decisions per trick (the decisions were not chosen with these features in mind), so most ranges are wide; like every group, their curves use the trick's shared exponent. Players hold fewer cards as the hand goes on, so hands with no void get rare (decisions with no void: 52 at trick 2, 5 at trick 3, 0 at trick 4). The trick-1 set can sample more decisions in a group that turns out to need many deals (M3-SPEC §13.1 item 9).

Rollout-PIMC against the exact yardstick (trick 2)

Rollout-PIMC is the cheap early-trick teacher: instead of solving each imagined deal exactly, it plays each deal out with everyone following the simple rules bot (rules-v1). Here its choices, with 8, 16, 32, 64 deals of its own, are scored against exact PIMC with all 320 deals (independent deals, so the referee does not flatter it).

  • Agreement: with 64 deals rollout-PIMC picks one of exact PIMC's best cards in 61% of decisions.
  • Money: it loses 0.35% money chance per decision on average (range 0.19%–0.62%), about 13× what exact PIMC with the same 64 deals is predicted to lose (0.027%).
  • More deals barely help: 8 deals: 53% agree, loss 0.47%, 16 deals: 55% agree, loss 0.37%, 32 deals: 58% agree, loss 0.38%, 64 deals: 61% agree, loss 0.35%. The error comes from assuming everyone plays like the rules bot, not from too few deals.
  • Position matters: positions 1–4 lose 0.60% on average, positions 5–8 0.09%. Losses are lopsided: the single worst decision (decision 195, pos1) loses 47% money chance on its own, which dominates that position's average, hence its wide range.

Trick 2

400 decisions, 320 exactly solved deals each; fair referee = 160 deals; curve fitted on N up to 80; 400 random splits per decision; ranges from 1000 bootstrap re-draws of the decisions.

  • Exponent b = 0.74 (95% range 0.61–0.94): doubling the deals cuts the expected loss by about 40%.
  • Fitted on different ranges of N the exponent stays put (up to N = 40: 0.76, up to N = 80: 0.74, up to N = 150: 0.72), so the curve is not bending within the measured range.
  • Held-out check: fitted on N ≤ 80 only, the curve predicted the measurements for with N between 80 and 160 inside their 95% band 63 times out of 63 (all decisions and the 8 positions); on average the prediction was 1.06× the measurement.
  • Extrapolation check: the same recipe run on only the first 160 deals (b = 0.73, range 0.55–0.98) predicted the 320-deal measurements inside their band 134 times out of 135, averaging 1.00× the measurement.
  • All decisions: about 243 deals for 0.01% (range 119–563), 622 for 0.005%, 2,154 for 0.002%.

The three readings of the measured loss, side by side

Split-half is what the curve is fitted to. The plain reading (random N deals judged against all 320) reads low as N approaches 320, because its referee shares deals with the player. The first-N reading is the single nested run the agreement report uses: noisy, since it is one draw.

Trick 3

400 decisions, 320 exactly solved deals each; fair referee = 160 deals; curve fitted on N up to 80; 400 random splits per decision; ranges from 1000 bootstrap re-draws of the decisions.

  • Exponent b = 0.71 (95% range 0.55–0.94): doubling the deals cuts the expected loss by about 39%.
  • Fitted on different ranges of N the exponent stays put (up to N = 40: 0.74, up to N = 80: 0.71, up to N = 150: 0.70), so the curve is not bending within the measured range.
  • Held-out check: fitted on N ≤ 80 only, the curve predicted the measurements for with N between 80 and 160 inside their 95% band 61 times out of 63 (all decisions and the 8 positions); on average the prediction was 0.97× the measurement.
  • Extrapolation check: the same recipe run on only the first 160 deals (b = 0.81, range 0.57–1.18) predicted the 320-deal measurements inside their band 127 times out of 135, averaging 0.88× the measurement.
  • All decisions: about 179 deals for 0.01% (range 84–456), 475 for 0.005%, 1,729 for 0.002%.

The three readings of the measured loss, side by side

Split-half is what the curve is fitted to. The plain reading (random N deals judged against all 320) reads low as N approaches 320, because its referee shares deals with the player. The first-N reading is the single nested run the agreement report uses: noisy, since it is one draw.

Method notes (for the record)

  • Choices are made exactly as the PIMC bot makes them (largest rounded fixed-point mean, ties to the first card); losses are exact integer differences in units of 2−32; only the statistics are floating point.
  • Split-half reading: for split s, a seeded permutation of the M = 320 deals; the first N choose, the first K = 160 make the reference choice, the last 160 score both. Its expectation is exactly L(N) − L(K), whatever the shape of the curve. The fitted model is a(N−b − K−b).
  • Fit: weighted least squares on log scale over N ≤ K/2, each point weighted by its share of the log-N axis divided by its squared relative standard error; b shared over the eight positions (profile search), a per group; other groups get their own a with the trick's b. N for a threshold θ is (a/θ)1/b.
  • Uncertainty: stratified bootstrap of decisions within position × situation cells; every fit redone per replicate; ranges are the 2.5% and 97.5% points.
  • Decisions are an equal mix of positions and match situations, not their natural frequencies; "all" is the plain average over that mix.
  • Hand features (the 5 of trumps, robber, voids) are worked out from what the deciding player can see: the robber flag comes from the public record of who burned a card (or must burn one now), never from hidden cards. Records saved before these features existed get them by replaying each decision from its decision file (--decisions), with no new solving. The comparisons between two groups are ratios of their N, with ranges from the same bootstrap re-draws (paired).
  • Reproduce: search curves --worlds exact-t3-n320.jsonl --decisions decisions-t3.jsonl --json curves-t3.json (likewise the other tricks); search score --yardstick exact-t2-n320.jsonl --n 320 --method rollout-t2-l2-n64.jsonl:8 …:64 --json score-t2.json; then uv run python/tools/ncurves_report.py --out docs/m3-ncurves --score score-t2.json curves-t2.json curves-t3.json curves-t4.json. The text tables are in curves-t*.txt and score-t2.txt next to this page. Extend chosen decisions: search worlds … --ids 3,17,42 --from-world 320 --to 640, then pass both worlds files to search curves.
